t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.3.texto: Paraphrase. Gilgamesh and Enkidu stop at the edge of the forest and gaze at the height of the cedars and the well-trodden path along which Humbaba walks. The mountain of cedars is the dwelling of the gods and the throne of Irnini; the cedars give off a pleasant shade and an intense fragrance. In the fragment discovered in 2011, the forest is full of noises: the birds sing, the monkeys shriek, the cicadas buzz, like an orchestra for its guardian. Humbaba confronts the heroes; Shamash unleashes thirteen winds that pin him down. Defeated, Humbaba pleads with Gilgamesh, offers to be his servant and to fell the trees for him; Enkidu insists on killing him before Enlil finds out. Humbaba curses them and they cut off his head. Then they fell the cedars, and from the largest one Enkidu makes a door for Enlil's temple at Nippur. They go down the river on a raft carrying Humbaba's head.
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.3.fuente: Paraphrase based on the editions by George (2003) and by F. N. H. Al-Rawi and A. R. George, "Back to the Cedar Forest: The Beginning and End of Tablet V of the Standard Babylonian Epic of Gilgameš", Journal of Cuneiform Studies 66 (2014)
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.3.nota_academ: Tablet V was very fragmentary in Thompson's day. In 2011 the Sulaymaniyah Museum (Iraqi Kurdistan) acquired a Neo-Babylonian tablet that adds some 20 lines, published by Al-Rawi and George (2014): it describes the forest as a living, resounding space and presents Humbaba almost as a foreign king. Humbaba (Sumerian Huwawa) was appointed guardian by Enlil, protected by seven terrible "auras" or radiances (melammū). In the Sumerian poems the forest lies to the east (the Zagros); in the standard version it is located in Lebanon.
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.3.lectura_ast: In The Stairway to Heaven (1980) Sitchin identifies the Cedar Forest with a "landing place" of the Anunnaki at Baalbek (Lebanon) and presents Humbaba as a mechanical or robotic guardian equipped with rays.

The text describes a natural forest (trees, fragrance, animals) whose wood was highly coveted in a Mesopotamia without forests; royal expeditions for cedar from Lebanon are documented from Sargon of Akkad on. Humbaba's "auras" are the melammu, the terrible radiance that characterizes gods and monsters throughout Akkadian literature. The great stones of Baalbek belong to a Roman temple of the 1st century AD.
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.3.lectura_act: Robert Pogue Harrison opens his cultural history of forests with Gilgamesh: the felling of the sacred forest and the death of its guardian mark the break between the city and the wild, and civilization is defined by the conquest of nature. The 2011 fragment, with its resounding forest, has strengthened these readings.
Robert Pogue Harrison, Forests: The Shadow of Civilization, 1992
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.4.texto:
(Now) he washes his stains, he cleans his tattered garments,
he braids (?) (the locks of) his hair (so that they fall loose) over his shoulders,
he lays aside his soiled clothes (and) puts on clean ones,
he puts on bracelets (?) and girds his body with a baldric;
Gilgamesh binds on the fillet and girds himself with a baldric.
(Then) the lady Ishtar beholds the beauty of Gilgamesh: (she says):
"Gilgamesh, come, be my husband; of the fruit (of your body) grant me bounty:
(for) you shall be my husband and I shall be your consort.
Oh, I will provide you with a chariot (all) of lapis lazuli and gold,
its wheel of gold and its yoke of precious stones, to be harnessed every day
to great mules: (oh), enter our house with the fragrance of cedar.
(So), when you enter our house, threshold and dais
shall kiss your feet, (and) at your feet kings, princes and lords shall bow down,
bringing you as tribute the produce of mountains and plains: your goats
shall bear in abundance, your ewes shall have twins, your asses shall reach
(each one) the size of a mule, (and) your steeds at your chariot shall win
renown for their gallop: [your mules] in the yoke shall never have a rival".
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.4.fuente: Spanish version based on R. Campbell Thompson, The Epic of Gilgamish (1928), p. 32, translated here into English from the Spanish
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.4.nota_academ: Ishtar's proposal (inbu, "fruit", has a sexual connotation) follows the language of marriage contracts and of sacred marriage rituals. Gilgamesh replies with a series of insulting comparisons that Thompson partly restored by conjecture (George: "a brazier that goes out in the cold, a back door that keeps out not the wind…") and with the catalog of Ishtar's lovers turned into animals or sent to the Underworld (Dumuzi among them). T. Abusch (1986) interpreted the offer as an invitation to become a god of the Underworld, that is, to die.
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.4.lectura_act: Rivkah Harris shows that in Mesopotamian literature Ishtar embodies paradox and the inversion of gender roles: it is she who proposes marriage and gives gifts, as a man would. The hero's rejection and Enkidu's mockery dramatize male anxiety in the face of an active female sexuality.
Rivkah Harris, Gender and Aging in Mesopotamia: The Gilgamesh Epic and Other Ancient Literature, 2000
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.5.ref: Tablet X, col. III (Thompson) = Old Babylonian Sippar version, col. iii
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.5.texto:
"Gilgamesh, why do you run, (if) the life you seek
you cannot find? (For) the gods, in their (first) creation of mortals,
allotted death to man, (but) life they kept in their own power.
Gilgamesh, fill your belly,
by day and by night be happy, (and) make a feast every day;
by day and by night dance and rejoice; (and) let your clothes be clean,
(yes), let your head be washed, (and) bathe in the water;
cherish the little one who holds your hand; let your wife in your bosom
be happy: (for) this is the portion [of man] […]".
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.5.fuente: Spanish version based on R. Campbell Thompson, The Epic of Gilgamish (1928), p. 46, translated here into English from the Spanish
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.5.nota_academ: This advice from the tavern keeper Siduri survives only on the Old Babylonian tablet from Sippar published by B. Meissner in 1902 (the "Meissner tablet"); in the standard version the scene was rewritten and the speech about death passed to Utnapishtim. Thompson inserted it into his Tablet X. Today it is translated essentially the same way. Its resemblance to Ecclesiastes 9:7–9 ("eat your bread with joy… enjoy life with the wife whom you love") is one of the most frequently cited parallels between Mesopotamian and biblical literature.
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.6.texto:
Utnapishtim (thus addressing) Gilgamesh replied:
"Gilgamesh, I will reveal to you the (whole) hidden story,
yes, and the design of the gods I will tell you. The city of Shuruppak
—(oh, it is) a city you know— lies [on the bank] of the Euphrates;
ancient is this city, with gods within it. (Then) the great gods resolved
to bring a flood: […] there was Anu, their father; their counselor,
the warrior Enlil; Ninurta, their herald; their chief (?), Ennugi;
Ninigiku —that is Ea—, (though) sworn with them,
to a reed hut revealed their counsel:
'O reed hut, reed hut! Wall, wall!
Listen, reed hut; reflect, wall! O you, mortal,
you of Shuruppak, son of Ubara-Tutu, pull down
a house (and) build (with it) a ship; abandon riches,
seek life (and) scorn your treasure, and save life; bring up
into the ship (the seed of) every creature. The ship that you shall build,
let its measurements be exact; let its width and its length correspond.
(Then) launch it [upon] the ocean'".
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.6.fuente: Spanish version based on R. Campbell Thompson, The Epic of Gilgamish (1928), p. 50, translated here into English from the Spanish
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.6.nota_academ: The flood story of Tablet XI was identified by George Smith in 1872 on tablets from Nineveh, and it adapts the Old Babylonian poem of Atrahasis (in line 196 the hero is called Atrahasis, "the exceedingly wise"). Ea does not break the gods' oath by speaking directly to a man: he speaks to the reed wall behind which Utnapishtim stands. The ship is a perfect cube (about 60 m on each side), with seven decks. The order "pull down the house, build a boat" can also be understood as a play on words for the reed hut, whose material serves for the ship. In line 140 Thompson reads "Mount Nisir"; the current reading is Mount Nimush (in Iraqi Kurdistan).
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.6.lectura_ast: Sitchin attributes the flood to the passage of Nibiru, which some 13,000 years ago would have caused the Antarctic ice sheet to slide and a gigantic wave; the Anunnaki would have watched the catastrophe from their ships in orbit, and Utnapishtim's ship would be a kind of submersible designed by Enki.

The Mesopotamian flood stories (the Sumerian one of Ziusudra, Atrahasis, Gilgamesh) date from between c. 1800 and 700 BC and reflect the experience of the floods of the Tigris and Euphrates; at Shuruppak, Kish and Ur there are layers of local floods from the beginning of the 3rd millennium. There is no geological evidence of a universal flood or of an Antarctic collapse 13,000 years ago, and the ship is described with the materials of the time: wood, reeds, bitumen, ropes.
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.6.lectura_act: George Smith's reading of the Gilgamesh flood before the Society of Biblical Archaeology (London, December 3, 1872) caused a sensation because it seemed both to confirm and to relativize Genesis. The Daily Telegraph funded his trip to Nineveh, where he found more fragments. It is the founding moment of popular Assyriology.
David Damrosch, The Buried Book: The Loss and Rediscovery of the Great Epic of Gilgamesh, 2007
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.7.texto:
Six days and seven nights the hurricane, the flood (and) the tempest went on
sweeping the land; when the seventh day came, the war ceased:
tempest (and) flood, which had fought like an army in battle array.
The sea grew calm, the gale was spent, the flood was stilled.
I looked at the day: (behold), every sound had been hushed, and all mankind
had returned to (its) clay, and the marsh was level with the roof.
I opened a hatch and the sunlight fell upon my cheek;
bowing down, I sat and wept, the tears ran down my cheeks.
I looked into the distance, to the farthest bounds of the ocean:
land emerged in twelve (places), and the ark ran aground on Mount Nisir;
Mount Nisir held it fast and would not let it move.
[…]
(Then), when the seventh day dawned, I brought out a dove and let it go;
the dove went and came back, (for) there was no resting place.
I brought out a swallow and let it go; the swallow went and came back,
(for) there was no resting place. I brought out a raven,
and let it go (as well); the raven went off, it saw the waters going down;
it ate, it splashed about, (and) did not come back (to me).
I let (all the animals) go to the four winds and made an offering.
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.7.fuente: Spanish version based on R. Campbell Thompson, The Epic of Gilgamish (1928), pp. 51–52, translated here into English from the Spanish
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.7.nota_academ: The parallel with Genesis 8:6–12 (raven and dove) is almost exact in structure. Next the gods, hungry after the flood, "gather like flies" over the sacrifice, and Ishtar (Belet-ili) swears by her lapis lazuli necklace never to forget those days. Thompson translates that mankind "had returned to clay", a reading that still stands. The mountain where the ark ran aground is read today as Nimush (not Nisir). In 2014 Irving Finkel (The Ark Before Noah) published an Old Babylonian tablet in which the ark is a huge round coracle, which shows that the shape of the ship varied between versions.
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.8.texto:
They broke their fast at the fortieth hour: at the sixtieth they rested.
Gilgamesh spied a pool of fresh water (and), going down into it,
bathed in the water. (But there was) a snake that sniffed the fragrance of the plant,
it came out [of the water (?)] and snatched the plant […]
as it withdrew. Then Gilgamesh sat down (and) burst into tears.
Over his cheeks ran his tears; to the boatman Urshanabi [he spoke]:
"(Tell me), [for] whom have my arms toiled, O Urshanabi?
for whom has the blood of my heart been spent? (Yes), not for myself
have I won the reward; (no), it is for a lion of the earth (alone)
that I have gained the prize".
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.8.fuente: Spanish version based on R. Campbell Thompson, The Epic of Gilgamish (1928), p. 56, translated here into English from the Spanish
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.8.nota_academ: The plant is called "the old man grows young" (šību iṣṣaḫir amēlu). Thompson confuses the measures: the numbers are double leagues (bēru), not hours ("at twenty leagues they ate, at thirty they camped"). Where Thompson has "casting a curse", the text says that the snake, as it left, shed its skin (ittadi qulipta): it is an etiology of why the snake grows young again and man does not. "Lion of the earth" (nēš qaqqari) is an expression for the snake. The episode closes the quest for immortality: all that is left to Gilgamesh is the fame of his work, the walls of Uruk.
t.textos.atrahasis.version: Old Babylonian version in 3 tablets (about 1,245 lines), copied by the scribe Ipiq-Aya around 1635 BC (reign of Ammi-saduqa); there are later Assyrian and Babylonian recensions (7th century BC)
t.textos.atrahasis.estructura.0.sinopsis: When the gods worked like men, the great gods (Anunnaki) divide up the universe and the lesser gods (Igigi) dig the rivers and canals. After 3,600 years they rebel, burn their tools and surround Enlil's temple at night. Enki proposes creating man: the mother goddess Nintu-Mami shapes him from clay mixed with the flesh and blood of the sacrificed god We-ila, who had intelligence. The first human beings are born.
t.textos.atrahasis.estructura.1.sinopsis: After 1,200 years humanity multiplies and its "noise" (rigmu) keeps Enlil from sleeping. He sends in turn a plague, a drought and a famine; each time the wise Atrahasis consults Enki, who teaches him how to deflect the punishment with offerings to the god responsible. Enlil, furious, decides on the flood and makes the gods swear not to reveal it.
t.textos.atrahasis.estructura.2.sinopsis: Enki warns Atrahasis by speaking to the reed wall. Building of the ship, boarding of the family and the animals; the flood lasts seven days and seven nights. The gods, deprived of offerings, suffer hunger and thirst; Nintu weeps for her creatures. After the sacrifice, Enlil is enraged to see survivors. Enki proposes controlling the population: barren women, the demon Pashittu who steals children, and priestesses who must not have children.
